title: CUET Political Science Test 9
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: A burden on India before the 1971 war
questions.question: Before the war of December 1971, India had to cope with:
options: A) about 80 lakh refugees from East Pakistan
B) a Chinese invasion across the McMahon Line
C) the withdrawal of all aid by the Soviet Union
D) a famine that spread over the whole of India
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) about 80 lakh refugees from East Pakistan
Why: The Pakistani army's crackdown in East Pakistan drove about 80 lakh refugees into India.
Why not the others:
(B) China did not invade in 1971.
(C) India signed a treaty of friendship with the Soviet Union in 1971.
(D) There was no nationwide famine in 1971.
Key point: The refugee burden pushed India towards supporting Bangladesh's freedom struggle.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Not part of Indira Gandhi's 'left turn'
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT part of the radical programme that Indira Gandhi followed in 1969–71?
options: A) Nationalising the major commercial banks
B) Moving to abolish the privy purses
C) Signing a military pact with the US
D) Calling for land reform and land ceilings
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Signing a military pact with the US
Why: Indira Gandhi did not sign any military pact with the US; in 1971 she signed a treaty with the Soviet Union.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) were all parts of her socialist programme against the Syndicate.
Key point: The left turn helped Indira Gandhi win popular support.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Korea from 1945 to 1996 in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Korean War comes to an end
(B) South Korea becomes a member of the OECD
(C) Korea is divided along the 38th parallel
(D) North and South Korea become members of the UN
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Why: (C) Korea was divided in 1945. (A) The Korean War ended in 1953. (D) Both Koreas joined the UN in 1991. (B) South Korea joined the OECD in 1996.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts UN membership before the end of the war. Option (B) puts the end of the war before the division. Option (C) puts OECD membership before UN membership.
Key point: 1945 → 1953 → 1991 → 1996.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: New body set up under the 2005 reforms
questions.question: Which body was created as part of the UN reforms agreed in 2005?
options: B) The International Court of Justice
C) The Economic and Social Council
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The Peacebuilding Commission
Why: The 2005 reforms created a Peacebuilding Commission, besides steps such as a Human Rights Council and a Democracy Fund.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are principal organs that date from 1945.
Key point: The 2005 summit was the UN's biggest reform effort.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Why India's stand in 1956 drew criticism
questions.question: Why was India's foreign policy criticised for its stand in 1956?
options: A) It sent troops to help Britain and France in the Suez Canal zone.
B) It joined a Western military alliance against the Soviet Union.
C) It led protests over Egypt but did not join condemning Hungary's invasion.
D) It refused to recognise the new government that had come to power in China.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It led protests over Egypt but did not join condemning Hungary's invasion.
Why: India led world protest against the British attack on Egypt over the Suez Canal, but did not join the public condemnation of the Soviet invasion of Hungary in the same year.
Why not the others:
(A) India opposed the attack on Egypt.
(B) India stayed non-aligned.
(D) India was among the first countries to recognise the People's Republic of China.
Key point: Critics said non-alignment was not always applied evenly.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: A founder of the Swatantra Party besides Rajagopalachari
questions.question: Besides C. Rajagopalachari, which of the following was among the leaders who formed the Swatantra Party in 1959?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Minoo Masani
Why: The Swatantra Party was formed by leaders such as C. Rajagopalachari, K.M. Munshi, N.G. Ranga and Minoo Masani.
Why not the others:
(A) Lohia was a Socialist leader.
(C) Kripalani founded the Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party.
(D) Dange was a Communist leader.
Key point: Swatantra stood for a free-market, pro-business position.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: EU member with a permanent Security Council seat
questions.question: Which member of the European Union holds a permanent seat in the UN Security Council?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) France
Why: France is a permanent member of the Security Council with a veto.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not permanent members.
Key point: France gives the EU a voice among the permanent five.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Environmental struggles and agreements
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Western Mining Corporation
(B) Narmada Bachao Andolan
(C) Franklin River
(D) Antarctic Environmental Protocol

List-II
(I) Mining company that faced protests in the Philippines
(II) Agreement of 1991 to protect a global common
(III) Indian movement against large dams
(IV) River whose damming was opposed in Australia
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: The Western Mining Corporation faced protests in the Philippines (I). The Narmada Bachao Andolan opposes large dams (III). Damming of the Franklin River was opposed in Australia (IV). The Antarctic Environmental Protocol was signed in 1991 (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the Narmada movement and the Franklin River. Option (B) swaps the Western Mining Corporation and the Narmada movement. Option (D) swaps the Franklin River and the Antarctic protocol.
Key point: Environmental movements are active all over the world.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Russia's status after the break-up
questions.question: After the disintegration of the USSR, Russia was accepted as the ________ state of the Soviet Union.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) successor
Why: Russia was accepted as the successor state and took over the Soviet seat in the UN Security Council.
Why not the others:
(B) A satellite state is one controlled by a bigger power.
(C) A buffer state lies between two rivals.
(D) A client state depends on a patron.
Key point: Russia inherited the USSR's international position.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: India and Pakistan, 1960–1972 — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Nehru and Ayub Khan signed the Indus Waters Treaty in 1960.
(B) The 1965 war began with Pakistani attacks in the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat.
(C) Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto signed the Shimla Agreement in 1972.
(D) India signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty when it was opened in 1968.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) Nehru and Ayub Khan signed the Indus treaty in 1960. (B) Pakistan launched attacks in the Rann of Kutch in 1965 before the larger offensive in Jammu and Kashmir. (C) the Shimla Agreement was signed in 1972.
Why not the others: (D) is false: India refused to sign the NPT, calling it discriminatory. Options (B) and (C) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Wars and agreements alternated in India–Pakistan relations.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Organisation that campaigned for the Ayodhya temple
questions.question: Along with the BJP, which organisation mobilised support for building a Ram temple at Ayodhya?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Vishva Hindu Parishad
Why: The Vishva Hindu Parishad, along with the BJP and the RSS, mobilised kar sevaks for building the temple.
Why not the others:
(A) The BSP drew its support from Dalits and did not lead this campaign.
(B) The CPI opposed the campaign.
(D) The DMK is a Tamil Nadu party.
Key point: The Ayodhya campaign put Hindutva at the centre of politics.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: The euro's challenge to the US
questions.question: According to NCERT, why is the euro significant for the US?
options: A) It has replaced the dollar in all trade between the US and Asia.
B) It is managed jointly by the US Federal Reserve and the EU.
C) It can pose a threat to the dominance of the US dollar.
D) It is the official currency of the United Nations system.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It can pose a threat to the dominance of the US dollar.
Why: NCERT says the euro can pose a threat to the dominance of the US dollar.
Why not the others:
(A) The dollar is still widely used in trade.
(B) The euro is managed by the European Central Bank.
(D) The UN has no single official currency.
Key point: The EU is an economic power that can rival the US.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Dimensions and critiques of globalisation — spot the error
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Globalisation has only an economic dimension and no political or cultural one.
(B) Under globalisation the welfare state tends to give way to a more minimalist state.
(C) Some critics describe economic globalisation as the re-colonisation of the world.
(D) In the colonial period India exported primary goods and imported finished goods.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: globalisation has economic, political and cultural dimensions.
Why not the others: (B) the welfare state gives way to a minimalist state. (C) some economists call it re-colonisation. (D) colonial India exported raw materials and bought finished goods. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Globalisation is multi-dimensional.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Military rule and democracy in Pakistan and Bangladesh, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) General Zia-ul-Haq takes power in Pakistan
(B) General Ayub Khan takes over the government of Pakistan
(C) General Pervez Musharraf takes power in Pakistan
(D) Democracy is restored in Bangladesh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (A), (D), (C)
Why: (B) Ayub Khan took over in 1958. (A) Zia-ul-Haq took power in 1977. (D) Democracy returned to Bangladesh in 1991. (C) Musharraf took power in 1999.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Musharraf before Bangladesh's return to democracy. Option (C) puts Zia before Ayub. Option (D) puts Bangladesh's democracy before Zia.
Key point: 1958 → 1977 → 1991 → 1999.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Life under the Soviet system — spot the error
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Soviet economy was more developed than that of every country in the world except the US.
(B) The Soviet state ensured a minimum standard of living for all its citizens.
(C) Soviet citizens were free to form political parties and compete in elections.
(D) The Soviet Union spent a large share of its resources on nuclear and military arms.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the Soviet system was a one-party state dominated by the Communist Party.
Why not the others: (A) NCERT says the Soviet economy was second only to the US. (B) the state guaranteed a minimum standard of living. (D) heavy military spending strained the economy. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The Soviet system combined welfare with authoritarian rule.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Institutions linked to economic globalisation
questions.question: Which international institutions are most closely associated with spreading economic globalisation?
options: A) The UNHCR and the ICJ
B) The IMF and the WTO
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The IMF and the WTO
Why: The IMF and the WTO have played a major role in opening economies and setting the terms of global trade and finance.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) deal with refugees, justice, children, health, culture and development, not trade and finance rules.
Key point: Critics say these institutions favour rich countries.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: UN body that organises environment conferences
questions.question: Which UN body has organised international conferences on the environment and encouraged studies on it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) UNEP
Why: The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) has organised conferences and promoted studies on environmental problems.
Why not the others:
(B) UNICEF works for children.
(C) UNHCR works for refugees.
(D) UNESCO works on education, science and culture.
Key point: UNEP helped put the environment on the global agenda.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Japan, South Korea, Denmark and Sweden, India — features
questions.question:
Match List-I (Country) with List-II (Feature).

List-I
(A) Japan
(B) South Korea
(C) Denmark and Sweden
(D) India

List-II
(I) Known as an 'Asian Tiger' for its rapid growth
(II) Home of brands such as Sony, Canon and Toyota
(III) Followed a 'Look East' policy from 1991
(IV) Resisted the Maastricht Treaty and the euro
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: Japan is home to Sony, Canon and Toyota (II). South Korea is an 'Asian Tiger' (I). Denmark and Sweden resisted the Maastricht Treaty and the euro (IV). India adopted the Look East policy in 1991 (III).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Japan and South Korea. Option (C) swaps South Korea and Denmark and Sweden. Option (D) swaps Denmark and Sweden and India.
Key point: Not every EU member accepted every step of integration.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Why critics worry about the poor
questions.question: Why do critics argue that economic globalisation can hurt the poor?
options: A) It stops the poor from buying any foreign goods at all.
B) It makes it illegal for workers to form trade unions.
C) It forces every poor country to close its borders.
D) The state withdraws from welfare, leaving them unprotected.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The state withdraws from welfare, leaving them unprotected.
Why: When the state cuts back on welfare and social protection, the poor lose the support they depended on.
Why not the others:
(A) Globalisation increases the supply of foreign goods.
(B) It does not ban trade unions.
(C) It opens borders rather than closing them.
Key point: Critics call for a social safety net for the poor.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Party that backed the Emergency
questions.question: Which of the following parties supported the Emergency declared in 1975?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Communist Party of India
Why: The CPI supported the Emergency, believing it was needed against a right-wing threat; it later called this a mistake.
Why not the others:
(A) Jana Sangh leaders were arrested.
(C) Socialist leaders were jailed for opposing it.
(D) The CPI(M) opposed the Emergency and its leaders were arrested.
Key point: Not every opposition party opposed the Emergency.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Actors in cooperative security
questions.question: Besides states, which of the following can be involved in cooperative security?
options: A) Only the armed forces of the five permanent members
B) Only the military alliances formed by the big powers
C) Only the national governments of developing countries
D) Bodies such as the Red Cross and other private groups
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Bodies such as the Red Cross and other private groups
Why: Cooperative security can involve international organisations, NGOs such as the Red Cross, businesses and well-known individuals.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) wrongly limit it to states or military bodies.
Key point: Non-traditional threats need many kinds of actors.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Mainstays of the Maldives' economy
questions.question: The economy of the Maldives depends mainly on:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) tourism and fishing
Why: Tourism and fishing dominate the economy of the Maldives.
Why not the others: The Maldives, a country of small islands, has no large oil, mining or heavy industry.
Key point: The Maldives is a small island economy.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Difficulty in drawing the Partition line — the exception
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the difficulties faced in carrying out the Partition of 1947?
options: A) All the princely states had decided to join Pakistan
B) Muslim-majority areas lay in two zones far apart
C) Not all Muslim-majority areas wanted to join Pakistan
D) Large minorities lived on both sides of the new border
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) All the princely states had decided to join Pakistan
Why: The princely states had not all decided to join Pakistan; most joined India. This was not a difficulty of drawing the line.
Why not the others:
(B) The Muslim-majority areas lay in the west and the east, so Pakistan had two parts.
(C) The North-West Frontier Province's leaders opposed the two-nation theory.
(D) Many Hindus and Sikhs were in areas going to Pakistan, and many Muslims in areas going to India.
Key point: There was no single Muslim-majority belt to separate cleanly.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Results of the break-up — the odd one out
questions.question: The break-up of the USSR had several results. Which one of these did NOT follow from it?
options: A) The confrontations of the Cold War came to an end
B) The Warsaw Pact grew stronger and admitted more members
C) Many new independent countries emerged in the region
D) Capitalism became the dominant economic system worldwide
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The Warsaw Pact grew stronger and admitted more members
Why: The Warsaw Pact was dissolved; it did not grow stronger.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are all consequences listed by NCERT.
Key point: The collapse changed the balance of power in the world.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Target of the Assam Movement
questions.question: The Assam Movement of 1979–1985 was directed mainly against:
options: A) the merger of Sikkim with India
B) the imposition of Hindi in Assam
C) the demand for a Punjabi Suba
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) illegal migrants from Bangladesh
Why: The movement, led by the All Assam Students' Union, demanded the detection and expulsion of illegal migrants, mainly from Bangladesh.
Why not the others:
(A) Sikkim's merger was not the issue.
(B) Language was not the main issue.
(C) The Punjabi Suba demand concerned Punjab.
Key point: The movement ended with the Assam Accord of 1985.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: How industrial countries secured resources in the Cold War
questions.question: During the Cold War, how did the industrialised countries try to secure the supply of key resources?
options: A) By stockpiling resources and keeping forces near supply sites
B) By handing control of all mines to the United Nations
C) By banning the import of raw materials from the South
D) By giving up the use of oil in favour of solar energy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) By stockpiling resources and keeping forces near supply sites
Why: NCERT says they deployed military forces near exploitation sites and sea lanes, stockpiled strategic resources and backed friendly governments.
Why not the others:
(B) The UN was not given control of mines.
(C) They depended on imports from the South.
(D) Oil remained central to their economies.
Key point: Resource geopolitics is about who gets what, when, where and how.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: New sources of threat — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Half the world's population growth is expected to occur in just six countries, including India and China.
(B) Human security puts the protection of states above the protection of people.
(C) India's internal security has been challenged by militant groups in regions such as Nagaland, Punjab and Kashmir.
(D) Migrants leave their countries by choice, while refugees flee war, disaster or persecution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A) NCERT says half the world's population growth will occur in six countries. (C) militancy in several regions has challenged India's internal security. (D) migrants move by choice, while refugees are forced to flee.
Why not the others: (B) is false: human security focuses on protecting people rather than states. Options (C) and (D) include (B); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Many security threats today are not military.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: India–Russia agreement of 2001
questions.question: What did India and Russia sign in 2001?
options: A) A treaty creating a joint Asian security alliance against China
B) A pact under which Russia joined the Non-Aligned Movement
C) An agreement to merge their two space research agencies
D) Around 80 bilateral documents under a Strategic Agreement
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Around 80 bilateral documents under a Strategic Agreement
Why: Under the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of 2001, the two countries signed about 80 bilateral documents.
Why not the others:
(A) No alliance against China was formed.
(B) Russia did not join NAM.
(C) The space agencies were not merged.
Key point: India and Russia share a vision of a multipolar world.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Countries most threatened by rising seas
questions.question: A rise in sea level caused by global warming would especially threaten countries such as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) the Maldives and Bangladesh
Why: Low-lying countries like the Maldives and Bangladesh could lose much of their land to rising seas.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are landlocked countries.
Key point: Global warming is a threat no country can tackle alone.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Backward-class and religious politics, 1980–1990, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Supreme Court gives its judgment in the Shah Bano case
(B) The National Front government falls
(C) The Mandal Commission submits its report
(D) Kanshi Ram founds the Bahujan Samaj Party
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: (C) The Mandal report was submitted in 1980. (D) The BSP was formed in 1984. (A) The Shah Bano judgment came in 1985. (B) The National Front government fell in 1990.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Shah Bano before the BSP. Option (C) puts the BSP before the Mandal report. Option (D) puts the fall of the National Front before Shah Bano.
Key point: 1980 → 1984 → 1985 → 1990.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Kerala's experiment in planning
questions.question: Kerala's 'People's Plan Campaign' was an experiment in ________ planning.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) decentralised
Why: Under the People's Plan Campaign, local bodies and people drew up plans themselves, which is decentralised planning.
Why not the others:
(B) Centralised planning is planning from the top.
(C) The campaign had nothing to do with defence.
(D) Private companies did not run it.
Key point: Kerala gave local bodies a big role in planning.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Areas of the World Bank's work
questions.question: The World Bank's work mainly covers:
options: A) peacekeeping, disarmament and arms control
B) refugee camps and the rights of children
C) setting rules for trade between countries
D) human development, farming and infrastructure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) human development, farming and infrastructure
Why: The World Bank works on human development (education, health), agriculture, the environment, infrastructure and governance.
Why not the others:
(A) Peacekeeping is handled by the Security Council.
(B) Refugees and children are the work of the UNHCR and UNICEF.
(C) Trade rules are set by the WTO.
Key point: The World Bank lends for development.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Leaders linked to Partition and integration
questions.question:
Match List-I (Person) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) Fazl Ali
(B) Bodhachandra Singh
(C) Osman Ali Khan
(D) Muhammad Ali Jinnah

List-II
(I) The Nizam who ruled the princely state of Hyderabad
(II) Headed the States Reorganisation Commission
(III) Led the Muslim League's demand for Pakistan
(IV) The Maharaja of the princely state of Manipur
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Justice Fazl Ali headed the States Reorganisation Commission (II). Bodhachandra Singh was the Maharaja of Manipur (IV). Osman Ali Khan was the Nizam of Hyderabad (I). Jinnah led the League's demand for Pakistan (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the Maharaja of Manipur and the Nizam. Option (B) swaps Fazl Ali and Bodhachandra Singh. Option (C) swaps the Nizam and Jinnah.
Key point: Integration involved both negotiation with rulers and redrawing of boundaries.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Planning and the rural economy — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Chaudhary Charan Singh argued that planning should give priority to agriculture and the villages.
(B) Land ceiling laws were enforced effectively, and big landowners could not keep surplus land.
(C) The Green Revolution widened the gap between classes and between regions.
(D) In the mid-1960s India faced a serious food crisis, with near-famine conditions in Bihar.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: land ceiling laws were not enforced well, and big landowners often evaded them.
Why not the others: (A) Charan Singh wanted agriculture-centred planning. (C) the Green Revolution helped some classes and regions more than others. (D) Bihar faced near-famine conditions in the 1960s. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Land reform lagged behind the plans' promises.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Year Goa became a State
questions.question: Goa, which had been a Union Territory after its liberation, became a full State of the Indian Union in ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1987
Why: Goa became a State in 1987.
Why not the others:
(B) Goa was liberated from Portuguese rule in 1961.
(C) The opinion poll on merger with Maharashtra was held in 1967.
(D) 1975 is the year Sikkim became a State.
Key point: Goa kept a separate identity through the opinion poll and later statehood.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: From the Bihar movement to the Shah Commission, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The government announces fresh Lok Sabha elections
(B) Jayaprakash Narayan leads a people's march to Parliament
(C) The Janata government appoints the Shah Commission
(D) Students in Bihar launch their protest movement
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D), (B), (A), (C)
Why: (D) The Bihar students' movement began in March 1974. (B) JP led the march to Parliament in March 1975. (A) Elections were announced in January 1977. (C) The Janata government appointed the Shah Commission in May 1977.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts JP's march before the Bihar movement. Option (C) puts the Shah Commission before the election announcement. Option (D) puts the election announcement before JP's march.
Key point: 1974 → 1975 → January 1977 → May 1977.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Regional movements and leaders
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

(D) Farooq Abdullah

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:

Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Dorji and the MGP. Option (B) swaps the Karbis and Dimasas and Dorji. Option (D) swaps the MGP and Farooq Abdullah.
Key point: Regional demands ranged from autonomy to merger.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System

(I) Official Congress candidate for President in 1969

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Party that won East Pakistan in 1970
questions.question: In the 1970 elections in Pakistan, which party won almost all the seats in East Pakistan?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Awami League
Why: Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman's Awami League won almost all the seats in East Pakistan, but West Pakistan's leaders refused to let it form a government.
Why not the others:
(A) The PPP of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto won in West Pakistan.
(B) The Muslim League was not the winner in the East.
(D) The Jamaat-e-Islami did not win the East.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: A ground for India's claim to a permanent seat
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the grounds on which India claims a permanent seat in the Security Council?
options: A) It has the largest military budget of all the member states.
B) It is the largest single contributor to the regular UN budget.
C) It has taken part in UN peacekeeping missions for a long time.
D) It was the only Asian country that signed the UN Charter.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It has taken part in UN peacekeeping missions for a long time.
Why: India points to its population, its growing economy and its long role in UN peacekeeping.
Why not the others:
(A) India does not have the largest military budget.
(B) The US is the largest contributor.
(D) Other Asian countries such as China also signed the Charter.
Key point: India's claim rests on population, economy and contribution to the UN.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Who led the peasant struggle in Telangana
questions.question: The peasant struggle against the Nizam's rule in the Telangana region was led mainly by:
options: A) the Muslim League and the Razakars
B) the Akali Dal and its local allies
C) the communists and the Hyderabad Congress
D) the Dravida Kazhagam and Periyar's followers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) the communists and the Hyderabad Congress
Why: NCERT says a peasant movement in Telangana, led by the communists and the Hyderabad Congress, rose against the Nizam.
Why not the others:
(A) The Razakars were the Nizam's armed volunteers who attacked the movement.
(B) The Akali Dal was a Punjab party.
(D) The Dravidian movement was based in Tamil Nadu.
Key point: Popular protest in Hyderabad came before the army's action in 1948.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Why India's smaller neighbours are wary of it
questions.question: Why are India's smaller neighbours often wary of it?
options: A) Its size and power make them fear it will dominate the region.
B) India has refused to take part in any regional organisation.
C) India has no trade or transport links with any of them.
D) India has demanded that they adopt its own Constitution.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Its size and power make them fear it will dominate the region.
Why: Because India is much bigger and stronger than the others, its smaller neighbours fear Indian dominance, which also slows regional cooperation.
Why not the others:
(B) India is a founding member of SAARC.
(C) India has extensive trade and transport links with them.
(D) India has made no such demand.
Key point: Size gaps make trust in South Asia difficult.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: The early party system — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Bharatiya Jana Sangh stressed the idea of 'one country, one culture and one nation'.
(B) The Socialist Party went through many splits, giving rise to parties such as the Praja Socialist Party.
(C) The Swatantra Party opposed development planning, nationalisation and the expansion of the public sector.
(D) Communist groups emerged in India in the early 1920s, inspired by the Bolshevik revolution in Russia.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B), (C) and (D)
Why: (A) the Jana Sangh spoke of one country, one culture and one nation. (B) the Socialists split many times, forming the Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party, Praja Socialist Party and Samyukta Socialist Party. (C) the Swatantra Party opposed planning, nationalisation and the public sector. (D) communist groups appeared in the early 1920s.
Why not the others: All four statements are correct, so options (A), (B) and (D), which each leave out at least one, are wrong.
Key point: The early opposition covered the whole ideological spectrum.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Number of States the Congress lost in 1967
questions.question: After the 1967 elections, in how many States was the Congress out of power, counting those where defections kept it from forming a government?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Nine
Why: The Congress lost its majority in seven States, and defections kept it out of power in two more, making nine States.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) do not match the seven-plus-two count given in NCERT.
Key point: 1967 showed the Congress could be defeated in the States.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Official name of the Mandal Commission
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The ninth general election, held in 1989, brought an end to what scholars had called the 'Congress system'. The Congress, which had won a record number of seats only five years earlier, was defeated, and no party won a majority on its own. A National Front government was formed with outside support from parties on both the right and the left. In August 1990 this government decided to implement a recommendation of the Mandal Commission, officially the Second Backward Classes Commission, which had been appointed to identify the socially and educationally backward classes and to suggest ways of advancing them. The decision set off violent protests against reservations in many cities of north India, but it also helped parties that drew their support from the backward classes to grow stronger. For many years afterwards, no single party could form a government at the Centre on its own strength. National parties had to seek alliances with regional and caste-based parties, and governments came to depend on partners who could bargain hard for their own interests. Some saw this as instability; others saw it as a sign that more groups now had a voice in power.

Question: According to the passage, what was the official name of the Mandal Commission?
options: A) The Second Backward Classes Commission
C) The National Commission for Minorities
D) The First Administrative Reforms Commission
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The Second Backward Classes Commission
Why: The passage says the Mandal Commission was officially the Second Backward Classes Commission.
Why not the others:
(B) The States Reorganisation Commission dealt with State boundaries in the 1950s.
(C) The passage does not mention a minorities commission.
(D) The passage does not mention administrative reforms.
Key point: The Mandal Commission was the second commission on backward classes.

options: A) To redraw the boundaries of the States on the basis of language
B) To conduct the general election after the fall of the Congress
C) To identify the backward classes and suggest ways of advancing them

options: A) The opposition parties withdrew all their support from the government at once.
B) Violent protests against reservations broke out in many cities of north India.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: What the passage implies about governing after 1989
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: What can best be inferred from the passage about politics at the Centre after 1989?
options: A) Regional and caste-based parties gained real bargaining power over governments.
B) National parties stopped contesting elections and left the field to regional ones.
C) Governments became more stable because every party now shared the same ideology.
D) Reservations for the backward classes were withdrawn because of the protests.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Regional and caste-based parties gained real bargaining power over governments.
Why: The passage says national parties had to seek alliances with regional and caste-based parties and that governments depended on partners who could bargain hard, so these parties gained leverage.
Why not the others:
(B) National parties kept contesting; they had to find allies.
(C) The passage says some saw the period as unstable, and does not say ideologies merged.
(D) The passage does not say reservations were withdrawn.
